learningObjectives.title: Overview of resource management: significance of food, water and energy
Changing demand and provision of food, water and energy in the UK
Water insecurity: patterns, causes and impacts
Increasing and managing water supply sustainably

questions.q: Which three resources does the AQA specification identify as fundamental to human development in this topic?
options: Food, water and energy
Food, water and shelter
Water, energy and minerals
Food, oil and timber
questions.explain: The topic examines the challenge of managing food, water and energy, all of which are essential to human wellbeing and development.

questions.q: What does the global inequality in resource supply and consumption generally show?
options: Higher income countries tend to consume far more resources per person than lower income countries
All countries consume resources equally per person
Lower income countries always consume more than higher income countries
Resource consumption is unrelated to a country's wealth
questions.explain: Wealthier, more industrialised countries have higher consumption per person, creating global imbalances between supply and demand.

questions.q: Why does demand for food, water and energy tend to rise as a country develops economically?
options: Rising incomes, industrialisation and population growth increase consumption
Resources become physically scarcer as a country develops
People need fewer resources when they become wealthier
Economic development has no effect on resource use
questions.explain: Economic development raises living standards and industrial activity, both of which push up demand for resources.

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'food miles'?
options: The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is consumed
The number of different countries a supermarket imports from
The weight of food a person eats in a year
The energy used to cook a meal at home
questions.explain: Food miles measure the distance food is transported, which is linked to its carbon footprint.

questions.q: Why has the UK's demand for imported food with a high carbon footprint increased?
options: Consumers want exotic and seasonal foods available all year round
The UK is no longer able to grow any of its own food
Imported food is always cheaper to produce than the equivalent UK crop
UK farms have stopped using any modern technology
questions.explain: Demand for out-of-season and exotic produce means more food is flown or shipped in, raising food miles and carbon footprint.

questions.q: What is 'agribusiness'?
options: Large-scale, industrialised farming run as a commercial business
A small family farm selling only at local markets
A scheme to reduce the amount of land used for farming
A government subsidy paid to organic growers
questions.explain: Agribusiness applies large-scale, capital-intensive, commercial methods to maximise food output.

questions.q: A UK shopper chooses to buy locally-grown, seasonal vegetables from a farmers' market instead of imported produce. This choice most directly reduces the food's:
options: Food miles and carbon footprint
Water surplus
Desalination costs
Energy mix
questions.explain: Local, seasonal sourcing shortens transport distances, lowering both food miles and the associated carbon footprint.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the pattern of water supply and demand in the UK?
options: The north and west have a water surplus while the south and east have a deficit
The south and east have a water surplus while the north and west have a deficit
The whole of the UK has a permanent water surplus
Water supply and demand are evenly balanced across the UK
questions.explain: The wetter, less populated north and west have surplus water, while the drier, densely populated south and east are in deficit.

questions.q: Why might a water transfer scheme be used within the UK?
options: To move water from areas of surplus to areas of high demand and deficit
To remove salt from seawater in coastal areas
To reduce the total amount of rainfall in the north
To increase food miles for imported produce
questions.explain: Water transfers redistribute water from surplus regions to deficit regions where demand outstrips local supply.

questions.q: How has the UK's energy mix changed in recent decades?
options: Reduced reliance on coal and increased use of renewables and gas
Increased reliance on coal and reduced use of renewables
A complete switch to burning only oil
No change at all in the sources used
questions.explain: The UK has cut coal use and expanded renewables and gas as it moves towards lower-carbon energy.

questions.q: What is one economic issue of exploiting more difficult energy sources such as fracking or offshore wind in the UK?
options: Extraction and development are often expensive, which can raise energy costs
It always makes energy completely free for consumers
It removes all need for imported energy immediately
It has no financial cost to companies
questions.explain: As easier reserves are used up, remaining sources are costlier to exploit, adding an economic challenge.

questions.q: An area where the available water supply is greater than demand is described as having a water:
options: Surplus
Deficit
Footprint
Transfer
questions.explain: A water surplus exists where supply exceeds demand; a deficit is where demand exceeds supply.

questions.q: Water insecurity occurs when:
options: The demand for water is greater than the supply of clean, reliable water
A region always has more water than it can use
A country produces all of its own food
Rainfall is evenly distributed throughout the year
questions.explain: Water insecurity means people cannot reliably access enough safe water to meet their needs.

questions.q: Which of the following is a PHYSICAL factor affecting water availability?
options: Climate and the underlying geology of an area
Over-abstraction of water by industry
Pollution of rivers by factories
Limited infrastructure caused by poverty
questions.explain: Climate and geology are physical factors, whereas over-abstraction, pollution and poor infrastructure are human factors.

questions.q: How can water insecurity harm human health?
options: Using dirty or polluted water spreads waterborne diseases
Clean water becomes more abundant
Food production always increases
Industrial output rises sharply
questions.explain: Where safe water is scarce, people use contaminated sources, spreading illnesses such as cholera and typhoid.

questions.q: A country builds a large dam on a river near its border, greatly reducing the flow reaching the country downstream. This situation is most likely to lead to:
options: Conflict over shared water resources
An increase in food miles
Lower demand for water downstream
A permanent water surplus downstream
questions.explain: Competing claims over a shared, limited river can create tension or conflict between the countries involved.

questions.q: What is desalination?
options: Removing salt from seawater to produce fresh water
Transferring water between two river basins
Recycling waste water from homes
Collecting rainwater from rooftops
questions.explain: Desalination treats seawater to make it drinkable, but it is energy-intensive and expensive.

questions.q: In a large-scale water transfer scheme, water is moved from an area of:
options: Surplus to an area of deficit
Deficit to an area of surplus
High demand to low population
Low rainfall to high rainfall
questions.explain: Transfers redistribute water from regions with plenty to regions that lack enough to meet demand.

questions.q: What is grey water recycling?
options: Reusing waste water from sinks, baths and showers for non-drinking purposes
Filtering salt out of seawater
Building large reservoirs behind dams
Importing bottled water from abroad
questions.explain: Grey water from washing can be reused for tasks such as flushing toilets or watering gardens, conserving fresh supplies.

questions.q: A community wants a sustainable, local way to improve its water supply. Which approach best fits this aim?
options: Rainwater harvesting and recycling grey water
Building a large multi-purpose mega-dam
Constructing an inter-basin water transfer
Installing a large coastal desalination plant
questions.explain: Small-scale, local techniques like rainwater harvesting and recycling conserve water sustainably with low cost and environmental impact.

specSource: AQA GCSE Geography (8035) specification; The Challenge of Resource Management
